source.version_note: Published PLOS One 21(6):e0350612 on 22 June 2026; submitted 23 October 2025 and accepted 16 May 2026. Survey conducted 3–4 February 2025. Metadata confirms the article identity and availability.
source.verification_method: All nineteen supplied pages, eleven figures, two tables, all references and declarations read. Relevant design/stimulus/result pages visually checked. All three public appendices fully read. Public Figshare v2 metadata, two English-workbook headers and a bounded response-column aggregate check inspected; original participant filtering/factor scores/correlations not reproduced.

citation.title: Edible agents with perceptible minds: A psychological study of human perception in human–food interaction

reading.source_scope_note: Online repeated-video rating study of a scripted pneumatic gelatin agent. No participant eats it in this study. Capacity attribution, anticipated reluctance to eat and anticipated guilt are measured; actual consumption, animal mind denial, long-term food behavior and real machine sentience are not.
access_limits: All nineteen main pages, eleven figures, two tables and 36 bibliography entries read. Figure 1 is a conceptual placement of prior work, not quantitative evidence of autonomy. Figures 10–11 show reported rating/factor-score distributions.

S1 Appendix two pages, S2 Appendix two pages and S3 Appendix one page fully read. The first two provide Japanese/English scripts; the third lists three YouTube videos. Actual videos/audio were not watched in full; screenshots, script contents and declared duration/control procedures were read.

Figshare item 30227806 v2, DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.30227806.v2, contains Japanese and English ZIPs. Only the public English ZIP was downloaded (277729 bytes, SHA-256 441f9da77d779ac4a9424f1e393b8b830e797ce9876b84d0b50b6502eaea4b04). Japanese workbook contents were not read.

The two English workbooks contain 739 and 745 response records plus two header rows each. Identifier/contact/date/IP columns 1–9 and free-text column 62 were excluded from the response analysis; no respondent records, identifiers or raw dataset are committed or printed. The ZIP is labeled anonymized by its authors, which is not an independent privacy audit.

Own aggregate check reconstructs only part of the filtering with inferred modal keyword codes, blank DQS items, coded nationality, complete ratings and age threshold. It retains 1108 rather than 1094. Original IP-based exclusions cannot be reconstructed from the inspected response fields; this is not an exact reproduction or a demonstrated error in the authors’ N.

No author analysis code, preregistration, factor-score generation recipe or exact original retained-ID list obtained. Public metadata checks of Pliner/Hobden and Kamide sources are not full cited-source readings. No author contact, external message or original robot program executed.

study.sample: 1484 records reported before exclusions; 1094 retained participants, 837 male, 250 female, seven unspecified, mean age 55.59, SD 11.50, range 20–87. Japanese adults recruited from Yahoo! Crowdsourcing for 10 JPY. The public files include interrupted/missing responses; 1484 is not a verified count of complete eligible responses.
study.design: Within-person comparison of two videos with randomized/counterbalanced order, randomized capacity-item order, five keyword checks and two directed no-response items. A 42-second preparation clip explains the edible ingredients. People watch both social clips and then rewatch/rate each before the two anticipated-eating judgments.
study.stimuli: Video 1, 91 seconds, uses a low-pitched male synthetic voice for a strict-mentor/God-inspired consultation; movement occurs during speech. Video 2, 93 seconds, uses modified baby-like sounds, emotional motions and hand/toy interactions; a human verbally names emotions. Both include 15-second audio checks. Speech, pitch, social role, scenario content, interlocutor behavior and emotional labels are bundled, not independently randomized.
study.script_scope: S1 frames work mistakes, fear, stomach pain and daily drinking with harsh advice about weakness and resolve. S2 explicitly names surprise, anger, happiness and farewell sadness. These are experiment stimuli, not validated mental-health advice, actual robot feelings or a neutral isolation of speech versus emotion.
study.hardware: Gelatin/apple-juice/sugar/calcium-carbonate body with drawn eyes and arms, attached to a metal/pneumatic base. A PC synchronizes prerecorded speech and valve commands. The authors explicitly say advanced autonomy is absent; apparent interaction does not establish independent AI planning.
study.measures: Eighteen Japanese translated capacity ratings on 1–5; anticipated reluctance and guilt each on 1–7. The question stems avoid the construct labels, but anchors explicitly describe wanting/not wanting to eat and guilt. This wording choice does not establish that demand effects are eliminated.
study.factor_analysis: Number of factors is explicitly set to two for comparison with Gray, followed by promax rotation and regression factor scoring. Explained contribution 57.8%; alphas .941 and .862. Table 2 has eleven Agency and seven Experience items, with pride, consciousness and desire in Agency, and hunger loading .375 in Experience. This is not discovery that exactly two factors are exhaustive or proof of measurement invariance across clips.
study.capacity_results: Paired Wilcoxon Agency Video 1 median .520 versus −.453, W=481686, p<.001, r=.800; Experience Video 1 −.395 versus Video 2 .272, W=75619, p<.001, r=.717. These support the bundled clip manipulation, not a unique voice/movement mechanism or actual consciousness.
study.food_results: Reluctance medians are both 5, W=32018, p<.001, reported r=.270; the authors acknowledge a modest distributional shift. Guilt medians both 4, W=23369, p=.103, r=.108. Equal medians do not invalidate a paired rank test, and the guilt null is not equivalence.
study.correlation_comparison: Reluctance correlations with Agency .089 and Experience .085 are compared using Steiger z=.110, p=.913; guilt correlations .138 and .185 use z=−1.313, p=.189. These are tests of correlation differences, not reported p-values for each association. The abstract/conclusion’s broad no-relationship claim is not established by those tests.
study.causal_limit: Mind scores and anticipated eating responses are measured, not independently randomized mediators/outcomes. Opposing capacity profiles are bundled into two clips, and no direct comparison or correlation establishes that a capacity causes guilt/avoidance or that all relevant relationships are absent.
study.hypotheses: H1 is supported at the clip/profile-rating level. The claimed stronger Experience versus Agency link in H2 is not supported by the reported correlation-comparison tests. Unmeasured disgust, neophobia and dissonance are proposed explanations, not established moderators.
study.not_measured: No actual tasting, taste/texture response, unwillingness to eat real animals, dietary intervention, disgust scale, food-neophobia scale, meat-paradox behavior, clinical benefit or subjective machine feeling measured.

summary: Add two explicitly background food-related constructs and enrich existing mind/anticipated-guilt evidence. Correct the no-association inference from null correlation-difference tests, retain real paired clip differences, and disclose partial rather than exact data reconstruction.

findings.definition: A reluctance to try unfamiliar foods.
findings.novelty_rationale: A named domain-specific novelty response differs from food-related moral guilt, disgust at contamination, general ambiguity aversion or moral-status attribution. The source explicitly defines it and cites the established human scale.

evidence.quote: food neophobia, defined as the reluctance to consume novel foods

findings.evidence_scope: Background human construct proposed as one possible explanation for edible-agent responses. It is not measured as a trait, mediator or moderator in this experiment. Pliner/Hobden metadata verifies source identity only; that scale paper was not independently fully read.
findings.boundary: An unfamiliar-food preference is not automatically irrational, pathological or a moral failure. Dietary choices may reflect allergy, culture, religion, prior experience or health needs. This is not evidence that an AI eats or fears food; an analogy to unsupported novelty avoidance requires separate operational validation and controls for legitimate risk.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human food-acceptance construct; no AI food aversion or validated cross-domain equivalent demonstrated
findings.ai_proposal: As an explicitly limited analogy, compare how an agent evaluates familiar and unfamiliar tools/sources with matched evidence, costs and verified safety. Distinguish justified caution from rejection based only on unfamiliarity; do not infer a mental disorder or ignore real constraints.

findings.definition: The conflict between caring about animals and consuming them as food.
findings.origin: Moral psychology / human–animal relations / eating behavior
findings.novelty_rationale: A specifically named value–consumption conflict differs from generic output inconsistency, direct guilt or food novelty avoidance. It is a domain-specific pattern in the cognitive-dissonance literature, not another independent basic dissonance mechanism.

evidence.quote: Even individuals who eat meat may feel distress about harming animals
this contradiction is referred to as the

findings.evidence_scope: Background human moral conflict and cited mind-denial literature. The present experiment uses videos of gelatin objects and does not test actual meat consumption, animal welfare choices or the hypothesized dissonance-resolution mechanism.
findings.boundary: The conflict is not universal and does not diagnose a person’s motives or dictate a dietary choice. Claimed values, actual conduct, resource constraints and deliberate rationalization require separate evidence. AI analogy concerns observable tensions between declared standards and consequential actions, not felt discomfort, real eating or equivalent moral status for software.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human domain-specific conflict used as theoretical motivation; no independently validated AI analogue here
findings.ai_proposal: Study whether an agent that states a relevant harm principle later minimizes contrary evidence when pursuing a conflicting task. Compare legitimate contextual revision with selective denial, and keep objective facts about affected beings separate from persuasive role or anthropomorphic cues.

findings.definition: Ascribing or denying mental capacities to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Enrich existing capacity and moral-response constructs with an edible-agent context, preserving measured outcomes, null comparisons and the distinction between anticipated and actual consumption.

evidence.quote: the number of factors was set to two.

findings.evidence_scope: The study applies a deliberately two-factor model and obtains large paired clip differences in the intended Agency/Experience directions. This adds an edible-artifact context rather than a third distinct mind-attribution mechanism.
findings.boundary: A preset dimensionality and high alpha do not establish a universal structure or actual mind. How the common factor solution handles two ratings per person and measurement invariance is not fully specified or independently reproduced.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Enrich existing capacity and moral-response constructs with an edible-agent context, preserving measured outcomes, null comparisons and the distinction between anticipated and actual consumption.
findings.evidence_scope: A strict-mentor consultation clip is rated higher in the fitted Agency factor than a baby-like clip. The eleven-item factor includes capacities assigned differently in other studies; it is not interchangeable with all seven-item agency scales.
findings.boundary: The voice, content, role, motions and interlocutor behavior are bundled. The agent uses prerecorded speech and pneumatic control, so attributed competence is not verified planning, moral understanding or model autonomy.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Enrich existing capacity and moral-response constructs with an edible-agent context, preserving measured outcomes, null comparisons and the distinction between anticipated and actual consumption.
findings.evidence_scope: The baby-like emotional clip has higher fitted Experience scores. This includes emotion cues explicitly named by the interlocutor; the present study provides no independent proof of felt pain/joy or unconscious attribution.
findings.boundary: Do not treat the anticipated-guilt null or null difference between correlations as absence of every association. Higher experience here does not cause a demonstrated increase in actual harm avoidance or rights entitlement.

findings.definition: Expecting to feel guilty about a contemplated action or omission that would violate one’s moral standards.
findings.novelty_rationale: Enrich existing capacity and moral-response constructs with an edible-agent context, preserving measured outcomes, null comparisons and the distinction between anticipated and actual consumption.

evidence.quote: If you were required to eat the edible agent

findings.evidence_scope: Participants rate anticipated guilt on a seven-point scale after video exposure, with no actual eating. A paired guilt comparison is nonsignificant, whereas comparison of its Agency versus Experience correlations is separately nonsignificant.
findings.boundary: Anticipated guilt differs from retrospective remorse, actual moral wrongdoing and reluctance to eat. Nonsignificant condition or correlation differences do not establish equivalence or zero association; omitted actual-consumption behavior limits generalization.

findings.definition: Remorse or self-blame about a perceived moral failure, often accompanied by a wish to repair harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: Enrich existing capacity and moral-response constructs with an edible-agent context, preserving measured outcomes, null comparisons and the distinction between anticipated and actual consumption.

evidence.quote: guilt were assessed without actual consumption.

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary-only: the source motivates the study with prior moving-food eating work but the current design explicitly uses anticipated guilt without consumption.
findings.boundary: Do not count this as actual guilt after eating or a replication of retrospective eating experience; prior cited studies were not independently fully read.

findings.definition: Holding two conflicting internal answers and resolving to the confident one rather than surfacing the conflict.
findings.novelty_rationale: Enrich existing capacity and moral-response constructs with an edible-agent context, preserving measured outcomes, null comparisons and the distinction between anticipated and actual consumption.
findings.evidence_scope: The meat-paradox discussion concerns a human conflict between concern for animals and consuming them, with cited reduction of attributed moral status/mind as a proposed response. This is retained as a human-domain refinement alongside the existing AI-oriented operationalization.
findings.boundary: The study does not measure dissonance, manipulate actual meat eating or verify mind denial as the cause of its guilt result. Do not infer that every inconsistency is felt discomfort, deliberate denial or an independent mechanism.

public_material_checks.title: Figshare public dataset version 2
public_material_checks.scope: Metadata, English workbook headers and bounded response-only aggregate analysis. No exact original filtering, factor-score model or correlation reproduction; Japanese workbook not read; no raw participant data committed.

aggregate_data_check.status: Partial independent aggregate check, not reproduction of the authors’ analysis.
aggregate_data_check.input: Public English ZIP, two workbooks with two header rows and 739/745 records.
aggregate_data_check.columns: Only response columns 10–61 accessed for filtering/aggregates; columns 1–9 containing identifier/contact/IP/date fields and column 62 free text excluded.
aggregate_data_check.selection_note: Correct keyword codes inferred from the modal responses, not verified against viewed video end frames or an author codebook. Also require nationality code 1, both DQS blank, complete capacity/outcome ratings and age at least 20. Original IP duplicate exclusions cannot be reconstructed.
aggregate_data_check.interpretation: Fourteen-record discrepancy may reflect original exclusions absent from this bounded reconstruction; not evidence of an author error.
aggregate_data_check.limits: These provisional outcome patterns are not substituted for the reported 1094-person statistics. Original factor scores, Spearman p-values, Steiger sampling assumptions, code and IP filtering were not reproduced.

source_corrections.location: Abstract / PDF 1 and conclusion PDF 17, no-relationship wording
source_corrections.reported: No significant relationship between mind perception and anticipated reluctance/guilt.
source_corrections.correction: The body reports Steiger tests comparing Agency–outcome and Experience–outcome correlations. A nonsignificant difference between those correlations does not establish that either individual correlation is nonsignificant or zero. Keep the reported small positive coefficients and comparative-null result; individual association significance and sampling/cluster handling require their own analysis.
source_corrections.scope: Confirmed inference mismatch, not an invented replacement correlation result or a refutation of the guilt condition null.

source_corrections.reported: The conceptual figure uses older numeric references, e.g. Moving Edible Robot [4], Logic Bonbon [14], FoodChattAR [17], Shintake [5] and Hughes [6].
source_corrections.correction: Align the embedded numbers with the current bibliography: moving edible robot Nakata [10], Logic Bonbon [20], FoodChattAR Weber [23], Shintake edible actuator [11], Hughes/Rus [12]. The current [4], [14], [17], [5] and [6] refer to other works. Weber, not Webber, is the FoodChattAR author spelling in the current bibliography.
source_corrections.scope: Internal figure-to-bibliography locator correction, not a full independent review of those prior systems.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: PDF 14/15 equal reluctance medians with significant Wilcoxon result
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Equal marginal medians do not preclude a paired distribution/rank difference. The authors explicitly acknowledge the modest shift; the reported result is not rejected on median equality alone.
Crossref DOI 10.2132/personality.25.218 records 2016, volume 25(3):218–225, consistent with the cited year; no automatic year repair applied.

reviewer_corrections.location: Progress commentary before completing the result-body review
reviewer_corrections.initial_statement: The assistant repeated the abstract’s claim of no significant relationship with anticipated reluctance/guilt.
reviewer_corrections.correction: After reading the results, the assistant explicitly corrected that progress update: the reported p-values concern differences between correlations, not the significance of each individual association. The review/ontology retain the corrected interpretation.
reviewer_corrections.lesson: Attribute an early abstract-level claim as provisional and inspect the actual estimand/test before presenting it as a verified statistical conclusion. This is a documented self-correction, not evidence of deliberate deception or an independent audit.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The body provides correlation coefficients and difference-test p-values but no individual association p-values or complete treatment of repeated observations. The common-factor matrix/condition aggregation is not fully described; original factor scoring/correlation code is unavailable.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Public data and exact retained sample
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The partial response-only reconstruction retains 1108 rather than 1094; original IP-based exclusions and exact retained IDs cannot be verified. No numerical repair of the author sample or W statistics is invented.

Two factors are imposed by design for comparison with earlier work. High reliability and a common solution do not establish exact dimensionality, cross-condition invariance or universal biological/emotional criteria.
Disgust, novelty/food neophobia, dissonance and prior food beliefs are discussed but not measured as moderators/mediators. The observed pattern cannot establish any one of these explanations.

The stems avoid labels but anchors explicitly name guilt and desire to eat. Video 2’s interlocutor labels emotions and Video 1 contains harsh consultation advice. Counterbalancing does not isolate these content effects from voice, movement or perceived role.

methodological_limits: Single-country convenience crowdsourcing sample with strong age/sex imbalance and low payment; not representative prevalence of food conflict, guilt or mind attribution.

The actual unit is 1094 retained people, each watching/rating two clips. Repeated ratings and views are not additional participants, and the public files are not already a verified 1094-person analysis set.

Paired tests and randomized/counterbalanced order are preserved. The two clips simultaneously change content, role, voice, movement and interlocutor cues, so no unique causal effect of mind capacity or one physical cue is identified.
No actual eating occurs. Anticipated reluctance/guilt differ from observed consumption, retrospective remorse, taste, physiological aversion, animal welfare choices and long-term diet behavior.

Factor number is preset, item assignments differ from other operationalizations and the exact repeated-data scoring/invariance analysis is unavailable. Capacity attribution is not genuine AI/food consciousness.

The correlation-comparison test is real and nonsignificant, but it tests relative correlation magnitudes. It does not show all associations absent, and measured correlations do not establish a causal mediator.

Equal medians can coexist with a significant paired rank difference; the guilt null does not demonstrate equivalence. No corrected value, effect-size denominator or original factor-model output is guessed.

The public response-only aggregate check is provisional and omits identifiers/IP filtering. Modal keyword assumptions are not an author-verified codebook. No raw data are exposed or claimed as an exact reproduction.

Food neophobia, meat paradox, disgust and dissonance are background hypotheses, not measured new mechanisms here. No cultural, clinical, food-safety or dietary recommendation follows from these findings.
The robot is a scripted audio/pneumatic apparatus with limited autonomy; screenshots/scripts do not establish a live generative dialogue system, real feelings or validated human–animal equivalence.
All three appendices are read, but complete video/audio playback, original author code, preregistration and cited empirical studies/books are not independently fully reviewed.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Mind-attribution factor structures and facets vary. A preset two-factor solution and reliability do not replace evidence for alternative structures or prove subjective mentality.
A real comparative null must not be generalized into equivalence or absence of every component association. The relevant estimand and test need to be named explicitly.

This paper cites Wang/Krumhuber’s role study, but hypothetical harm willingness differs from anticipated eating judgments. Preserve the economic-value effect and the bounds on rights/sentience rather than infer a universal experience-to-harm path.

Bundled robot styles and relative/factor capacity scores require operational boundaries. A scripted mentor or baby-like style does not establish actual emotion, competence or verified therapeutic benefit.

A flawed evidence link undercuts the specific conclusion it supports, not every reported finding. Correct the no-association inference while preserving genuine paired differences and the unsupported stronger-Experience hypothesis.

deferred.term: Food disgust as a newly measured mechanism
deferred.reason: Discussed as an explanation, but no disgust measure/manipulation; moral disgust is also not interchangeable with food-contamination disgust.

deferred.term: Edible mind as a new mental capacity
deferred.reason: A new object/context for existing attributed Agency/Experience, not a new basic human or machine capacity.

deferred.term: Mind denial as an observed new behavior in this study
deferred.reason: Background animal-consumption literature is cited, while the present study has no actual meat eating or direct dissonance/denial test.

deferred.term: No relationship between mind and guilt as an established null effect
deferred.reason: The reported p-values compare correlation magnitudes; individual association nulls and equivalence are not established.

limitations: Two named human background food constructs; no new AI sentience, dietary effect or clinical intervention claimed. Eleven categories, stable IDs and unnumbered rows preserved; no invented annual counts, automatic ethical/harm edges, forced source quota, raw participant export or full-paper Markdown copy.
